newsitem.title: USA: IBM, Apple to discuss Mac licensing -source.
newsitem.headline: IBM, Apple to discuss Mac licensing -source.

text.p: International Business Machines Corp executives will meet counterparts at Apple Computer Inc Wednesday to renegotiate licensing fees for Macintosh software, an executive close to the talks said.
IBM, disgruntled about Apple's decision to raise the royalty it charges other computer makers for the right to use Mac software, will ask its long-time partner for a break, the executive said.
IBM declined to comment. Apple officials could not immediately be reached for comment.
"Unless the licensing fees come down significantly, IBM will back away from its effort to license the Mac OS," said the executive, referring to the Mac operating system.

Apple allows other computer companies to use its Mac operating system -- a type of program that handles the basic fuctions of the computer -- for a fee. IBM licenses the Mac software but currently does not make Mac-compatible machines.
Instead, IBM resells the Mac software, along with the PowerPC chip, to other Mac clone-makers.
Apple, financially strapped and still looking for new sources of revenue, is considering raising the fees it charges all clone makers, executives at the Cupertino, Calif. company have said.

Apple and IBM, along with Motorola Inc, set up the PowerPC alliance six years ago to develop microchips and software to provide an alternative to the so-called Wintel PC -- computers based on software from Microsoft Corp and chips from Intel Corp.
The alliance so far has failed to dent Wintel. What's more, Apple's decision to raise its Mac royalty has angered its PowerPC partners, executives close to the companies said.
Motorola, which makes Mac clones, also said it has been in ongoing talks with Apple about renegotiating its licensing fees.

"We are on the eve of a new deal here and we are excited about that -- as much as we are concerned that the price may go up," said Dennis Saloky, director of marketing programs in Motorola's Computer Products group.
Saloky said Motorola's licensing talks with Apple revolve around a new hardware design of the Macintosh, due sometime this summer.

"We are changing the hardware platform and it's inevitable that we have to change the licensing," Saloky said. "We have to renegotiate the licensing agreement anyway because the old license doesn't work."
